study.title: Exodus 15 - Song of Victory, Path in the Desert and Rest in Elim
study.overview: Exodus 15 brings Israel's response to liberation in the Red Sea and the first stage of the desert walk. The chapter begins with a song of celebration, in which Moses and the people proclaim that the LORD defeated the enemy with his power and saved Israel with his strong hand. Then the text extends the meaning of deliverance: God not only overcame Egypt, but revealed who he is holy, incomparable, eternal king and guide of his people. After praise, the narrative descends to the test of the desert: lack of water, there is murmuring, God turns bitter waters into sweets, and then leads the people to Elim, where there is an abundance of water and rest.

outline.title: Song of Moses: The LORD defeats Egypt
outline.explanation: The initial verses form the core of the song. Moses and Israel speak as one people, celebrating that the Lord threw into the sea the chariots, horsemen and leaders of Egypt. The text highlights the absolute superiority of God: it is strength, salvation, powerful warrior, holy and wonder operator. Victory is not attributed to human capacity, but to the direct intervention of the LORD.

outline.title: God leads and establishes his people
outline.explanation: The second part of the song shows that deliverance has a future purpose. Not only does God destroy the enemy; he leads the rescued people to their inheritance and to their abode. Neighbouring peoples are taken from fear, and the final horizon is the installation of Israel in the place prepared by God. The climax is the claim that the Lord will reign forever.

outline.title: Memorial of crossing, praise of Miriam and test in Mara
outline.explanation: Verse 19 summarizes the crossing of the sea as a contrast between the destruction of Egypt and the dry passage of Israel. Then Miriam leads the women in a liturgical response of praise. The narrative then changes to the desert: three days without water, bitter waters in Mara, murmuring of the people, intercession of Moses and the healing of the waters through a tree. There God establishes statutes and proof Israel, linking obedience to health and fidelity to his voice.

outline.title: Elim: provision and rest
outline.explanation: The chapter ends with a concrete relief: Elim, where there are twelve fountains and seventy palm trees. After the scarcity and bitterness, the people find a place of water and rest, a sign of divine provision on the way to the desert.

study.context: The notes indicate that the song of Exodus 15 is considered by scholars one of the oldest preserved compositions of the Hebrew language, and which was sung by Moses and the sons of Israel shortly after the defeat of the Egyptian army. The chapter shows the immediate passage of the celebration for the journey in the desert of Sur, where the lack of water and the experience of Mara make visible the fragility of the newly opened people. The mention of Miriam also shows that praise had community expression, with the participation of women.
study.theology: The chapter teaches that salvation belongs to the LORD from beginning to end. He frees with power, but also forms his people on the way. The song insists that God is incomparable: it is not only stronger than the gods of the nations, but holy, glorious and worthy of praise. The crossing of the sea and the collapse of Egypt reveal that arrogant human projects do not resist the breath of God. At the same time, Mara and Elim show that faith in God does not eliminate proof; it learns to depend on his word. The link between obedience and health in verse 26 should be read as a covenant guidance and not as a mechanical formula. The chapter ends by pointing to the permanent reign of the LORD: historical liberation already anticipates its lasting sovereignty over the people and on history.

scholarViews.insight: The song is treated as one of the oldest compositions preserved in Hebrew, which underlines its importance in the faith and memory of Israel.
Moses led the people to sing immediately after the victory, so that the deliverance received would be celebrated with gratitude and adoration.
The verse states that whoever has the LORD as strength will also have him as a song; true worship is born of the salvation received.

questions: What changes in the worship of Israel when the people come from remembering deliverance to sing God's own experience as their God?
How does the murmuring in Mara reveal the difference between seeing a miracle at sea and relying on God in the desert?
How does the claim that the Lord reigns forever corrects our urge to attribute ultimate security to human powers?
study.practice: This chapter invites you to turn deliverance into worship and difficulty into dependence. We can practice this by specifically reminding God's actions in our history, praising him in community and seeking his direction before reacting with murmuring when there is a lack of provision. We are also called to obey God's voice in everyday life, trusting that his commandments are not arbitrary weight, but a way of life. Finally, Elim reminds us that God knows how to lead his people both through the wilderness and by times of rest; in both he remains the same Lord.
study.uncertainty: The notes provided do not explain in detail all the literary and historical aspects of the chapter, especially the exact identification of Elim and the precise reading of the relationship between obedience and health in Exodus 15:26. Some observations of the commentators, such as poetic divisions and possible symbolic correspondences of the number of sources and palm trees, are interpretations and cannot be treated as indisputable facts of the text.
